notes.7.1: The text’s eaodem, eui and marites are read as eaedem, cui and maritos.

nodes.text: Let us turn now to reviewing the actual reasons by which the apostle teaches that a woman ought to be veiled, [to see] whether the same apply also to virgins, so that from this too the sharing of the name between virgins and non-virgins may be established, when the same reasons for the veil are found on both sides. If the man is the head of the woman, surely of the virgin too, from whom comes that woman who has married, unless the virgin is a third kind, some monster that is its own head. If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved or shorn, surely for a virgin too. So let the world, God’s rival, look to it, if it falsely claims that cropped hair is becoming to a virgin, as hair let grow is to a boy. Therefore she for whom it is equally unfitting to be shaved or shorn, for her it is equally fitting to be covered. If woman is the glory of man, how much more the virgin, who is also a glory to herself? If woman is from man and for the sake of man, that rib of Adam was first a virgin. If woman ought to have power over her head, all the more justly the virgin, to whom the reason for it belongs. For if [it is] because of the angels, namely those whom we read fell away from God and heaven through desire for women, who can presume that such angels desired bodies already defiled and the leavings of human lust, rather than burning for virgins, whose bloom excuses even human lust? For Scripture too suggests this: ‘And it came to pass,’ it says, ‘when men had begun to grow more numerous upon the earth, and daughters were born to them, the sons of God, having seen the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, took for themselves wives from all whom they chose.’ For here the Greek word for ‘women’ has the sense of ‘wives’, because marriage is mentioned. When, therefore, it says ‘daughters of men’, it plainly indicates virgins, who would still be counted as belonging to their parents (for married women are named as their husbands’), when it could have said ‘wives of men’; likewise it names the angels not adulterers but husbands, since they take the unmarried daughters of men, whom it said above were born, thus too indicating virgins: above, ‘born’, but here ‘married’ to angels. I know them as nothing other than ‘born’ and then ‘married’. A face so dangerous, then, ought to be shaded, which has hurled stumbling-blocks as far as heaven, so that, standing before God, before whom it stands accused of the angels’ banishment, it may blush before the other angels too, and may at last restrain that evil freedom of its head, which ought now not to be offered even to the eyes of men. But even if those angels had sought women already defiled, all the more ought virgins to have been veiled because of the angels, as it was all the more possible for the angels to have sinned because of virgins. If, moreover, the apostle adds the prior verdict of nature, that abundance of hair is a woman’s honour because hair serves as a covering, surely this is above all the mark of a virgin, whose very adornment is properly such that, heaped up on the crown, it covers the very citadel of the head with a ring of hair.
